questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: The best creams to buy for perfect skin
Why teenagers eat unhealthy food
Acne and its effects, told partly by a doctor who had it herself
How to become a skin doctor
questions.why: They discuss acne and hear from a dermatologist who suffered from acne herself.

questions.q: At what age does acne often happen, according to Neil?
options: Between 14 and 19
Only after 30
Between 5 and 10 years
Only in old age
questions.why: Neil says it often happens between the ages of 14 and 19, but can continue into adulthood.

questions.q: Why can acne be especially hard during the teenage years?
options: Because teenagers can't buy medicine
Because teenagers' self-image and appearance are changing
Because acne is much more painful for younger people than for adults
Because schools don't allow make-up
questions.why: Beth says it's emotionally damaging when our self-image and physical appearance are changing.

questions.q: What does dermatologist Dr Sharon Crichlow say about acne in adults?
options: It almost never continues after the teenage years, even in severe cases
It only affects men
It is always mild in adults
In up to 20% of patients, mostly women, it lasts into their 30s and 40s
questions.why: She says in up to 20 or so percent, certainly in females, it persists into the 30s and 40s.

questions.q: Why does Dr Crichlow say acne should never be treated as unimportant?
options: Because it spreads easily
Because treatment is very expensive and most families can't pay for it
Because it can cause other diseases
Because even mild acne can hurt teenagers' feelings and friendships
questions.why: She says it has a huge psychological impact and affects teenagers' friendships and peer groups.

questions.q: What causes acne, according to Beth?
options: Eating too much chocolate
Natural hormones and genes, which cause oil and bacteria in the skin
Not washing your face often enough, especially after exercise or sport
Using too much make-up
questions.why: She says acne is largely genetic and the build-up of oil and bacteria is due to natural hormones.

questions.q: Why didn't Dr Crichlow see a dermatologist when she was young?
options: There were no dermatologists in Barbados
She was too embarrassed
Her family couldn't afford it
Her acne was very mild
questions.why: She says her family 'just simply couldn't afford it'.

questions.q: Why does Dr Crichlow tell patients she has tried the treatments herself?
options: To show she understands and can say from experience that they work
To sell them her own products
To explain why she became a doctor late
To warn them that some of the treatments can be dangerous if misused
questions.why: She says pretty much anything she recommends, she's tried herself and 'can tell them, it works'.
